introduction.p: The equation y^{\prime\prime}+\omega^2y=0 has sine and cosine solutions. Complex exponentials combine these oscillations in e^{i\omega t}, whose real and imaginary parts are \cos(\omega t) and \sin(\omega t). We will use this representation for constant-coefficient second-order equations.

subsection.title: The spring equation
subsection.p: Picture a mass m>0 attached to a spring on a frictionless horizontal track.
Positive y means the mass is displaced to the right. Negative y means the mass is displaced to the left.
Hooke’s law says that the spring force is proportional to displacement and points back toward equilibrium:
Here acceleration is the second derivative:
This is the simple harmonic oscillator.

figure.caption: A spring pulls back toward equilibrium. Newton’s law turns this restoring force into a second-order equation.

description.p: A spring pulls back toward equilibrium. Newton’s law turns this restoring force into a second-order equation.

subsection.p: So the acceleration always points opposite the displacement. When the mass is to the right, acceleration points left. When the mass is to the left, acceleration points right.
That is what makes the motion reverse.
A second-order equation needs two initial conditions. To know how the mass will move, we need both its initial position and its initial velocity:
Position alone is not enough. If the mass is at y=1, it could be moving right, moving left, or momentarily stopped. Those motions have different futures.

exercise.title: Why is a spring a second-order equation?

statement.p: Newton’s law plus Hooke’s law produce y''+\omega^2 y=0. In your own words, why does a restoring force become a statement about the second derivative, and why is position alone not enough to determine the future motion?

hint.p: Force determines acceleration, which is y''. The same position can be moving right, moving left, or stopped, so the initial velocity is a second piece of data.

exercise.title: Why are sine and cosine shadows of a rotation?

statement.p: The complex motion e^{i\omega t} satisfies the spring equation, and its real and imaginary parts are \cos(\omega t) and \sin(\omega t). In your own words, why does oscillation appear as the shadow of rotation, and why is the general real solution a linear combination of those two shadows?

hint.p: A rotating point in the plane projects onto two back-and-forth motions. Linearity lets you mix those two real solutions, which is enough to match any initial position and velocity.

exercise.title: What does it mean that energy is conserved?

statement.p: For the undamped spring, the quantity E=\frac12 m(y')^2+\frac12 k y^2 has derivative zero. In your own words, why is a conserved quantity a quantity whose derivative vanishes, and how does that explain the exchange between kinetic energy and spring potential?

hint.p: If E'=0, then E cannot change. At a turning point the mass is stopped and all the energy is potential; at equilibrium the spring is unstretched and all the energy is kinetic.

statement.p: A damping force opposing velocity produces E'=-c(y')^2\le 0. In your own words, why does that term make oscillation fade, and what role do complex characteristic roots play in describing the faded motion?

hint.p: Negative derivative of energy means the energy is decreasing whenever the mass is moving. Light damping gives complex roots whose real part produces exponential decay multiplying the oscillation.
